item.title: Assessment of Carotid Doppler Parameters to Evaluate Volume Status: A Prospective Observational Study
item.category: Journal of the American College of Emergency Physicians open
item.description:
Objectives: Accurate assessment of volume status and fluid responsiveness is essential to guide fluid therapy, as unnecessary fluid administration may lead to fluid overload and adverse outcomes. Carotid Doppler ultrasound has emerged as a rapid, noninvasive alternative to more technically demanding echocardiographic measures. This study evaluated the utility of carotid Doppler-derived corrected flow time (FTc) and velocity-time integral (VTI), and their changes after passive leg raise (PLR), in assessing volume status and preload responsiveness.

Methods: We conducted a prospective observational study during Ramadan at a tertiary academic medical center. A total of 202 participants were enrolled, including 103 fasting individuals assessed during presumed relative dehydration and after rehydration, and 99 nonfasting hydrated controls. Carotid Doppler measurements of FTc, VTI, and Vmax were obtained before and after PLR. Diagnostic performance of percent changes in FTc (ΔFTc) and VTI (ΔVTI) was evaluated using receiver operating characteristic analysis.

Results: Participants in the fasting group underwent a mean fasting duration of 12.4 ± 1.1 hours and consumed a mean of 920 ± 352 mL of fluid after breaking the fast. PLR induced significantly greater increases in FTc and VTI during presumed relative dehydration. A ≥10% increase in VTI was observed in 57.2% of presumed relative dehydrated participants compared with 26.3% of hydrated controls and 20.4% of rehydrated participants. Similarly, a ≥5% increase in FTc was observed in 47.6%, 17.2%, and 22.3% of participants, respectively. Receiver operating characteristic analysis demonstrated moderate discriminatory performance for presumed relative dehydration, with areas under the curve of 0.708 for ΔVTI and 0.715 for ΔFTc. Optimal cutoff values were 5.92% for ΔVTI and 5.05% for ΔFTc.

Conclusion: Carotid Doppler-derived FTc and VTI are promising noninvasive markers of volume status and preload responsiveness. ΔVTI demonstrated greater sensitivity, whereas ΔFTc provided higher specificity, supporting the potential role of carotid Doppler ultrasound as a practical bedside tool for hemodynamic assessment.

item.title: Constipation Not So Vibrant: A Case Report of Colonic Obstruction From Capsule Retention
item.category: Journal of the American College of Emergency Physicians open
item.description:
Vibrating capsules represent a novel, nonpharmacologic approach for chronic idiopathic constipation, with favorable safety profiles in clinical trials, showing no reported retention events. Although generally well tolerated, patients with severe motility disorders and use of narcotics pose risk of retention of capsules. We report a case of a 73-year-old woman with a history of gastroparesis and slow-transit constipation, who developed colonic retention of multiple vibrating capsules, requiring colonoscopic retrieval. Careful patient selection, monitoring, and timely imaging may prevent complications when treating patients with vibrating capsules.

item.title: Automated Calculation of the Pediatric Emergency Care Applied Research Network (PECARN) Intra-Abdominal Injury Rule from Unstructured Emergency Department Notes Using a Large Language Model
item.category: Journal of the American College of Emergency Physicians open
item.description:
Objective: The Pediatric Emergency Care Applied Research Network (PECARN) intra-abdominal injury clinical prediction rule identifies children at very low risk for clinically significant intra-abdominal injury after blunt abdominal trauma. However, retrospective evaluation of the rule's use in practice requires resource-intensive chart review. We investigated whether large language models (LLMs) can automatically calculate PECARN intra-abdominal injury risk scores from real-world unstructured emergency department (ED) notes.

Methods: We conducted a retrospective secondary analysis of children after blunt abdominal trauma presenting to 2 urban pediatric EDs. The LLM, OpenAI o1, was compared with clinician-derived standards for PECARN risk scores and predictor variable extraction from unstructured physician ED notes. Performance was assessed using standard diagnostic test characteristics.

Results: Among 196 children with complete ED notes, the LLM calculated binary PECARN risk scores with 95.4% accuracy (95% confidence interval [CI] 92.5 to 98.3), 94.4% sensitivity (95% CI 90.6 to 98.2), 98.2% specificity (95% CI 94.6 to 100), and an F1 score of 0.97 (95% CI 0.90 to 0.98). Agreement by weighted Cohen's kappa between multicategorical LLM-derived risk scores and clinician-derived risk scores was high, 0.96 (95% CI 0.92 to 1.00). Predictor variable extraction demonstrated strong performance across all PECARN variables, with accuracy greater than 94%.

Conclusion: The LLM had comparable performance to clinicians in calculating binary and multicategorical PECARN intra-abdominal injury risk scores and extracting predictor variables from unstructured ED notes. LLMs may enable automated calculation of clinical prediction rules from clinical documentation.

item.title: Alcohol-Related Emergency Department Visits of Young Adults in a University City in the Netherlands
item.category: Journal of the American College of Emergency Physicians open
item.description:
Objectives: This study aimed to examine the incidence and characteristics of alcohol-related emergency department (ED) visits in young adults compared with older age groups.

Methods: A retrospective electronic health record study of patients aged ≥18 years with an alcohol-related ED visit, including acute alcohol intoxication (AAI) and alcohol-related injuries, was conducted at Reinier de Graaf Gasthuis (RdGG) from January 1, 2022 to January 1, 2024. Young adults (18 to 24 years) were compared with older age groups (25 to 39, 40 to 54, 55 to 69, >70 years) regarding visit type, blood alcohol concentration (BAC), diagnostic tests, and hospital admission. Within young adults, student status and peak visit times were analyzed.

Results: Of 49,226 ED visits, 888 (1.8%) were alcohol-related, including 192 (21.6%) young adults, of whom 40% were students. Men were more frequently admitted with alcohol-related injuries (36.4% vs 25.4%), women for AAI (67.8% vs 47.3%, P < .001). Alcohol-related visits were highest among young adults (4.3% vs. 0.7-2.8%, P < .001). AAI was significantly more prevalent in the 18 to 24 group than in older groups. Most injuries in young adults involved head or neck trauma (84%). Students had higher mean BACs than nonstudents (2.34 vs 1.84 g/L, P = .019).

Conclusion: Young adults account for the highest incidence of alcohol-related ED visits. Students exhibit higher BACs than nonstudents. These findings underscore the critical need to reduce alcohol-related harm and promote safe drinking habits among young adults especially during specific periods.

item.title: Emergency Medical Technician Program Certification Pass Rates by Size and Geographic Region: A Five-Year Descriptive Analysis
item.category: Journal of the American College of Emergency Physicians open
item.description:
Objectives: Emergency medical technician (EMT) educational programs demonstrate student certification performance variability. Prior evaluations identified program size and regional disparities, yet whether these patterns persist is unclear. This study described national variation in EMT certification pass rates by cohort size, geographic region and cohort year.

Methods: We conducted a repeated cross-sectional descriptive analysis of United States civilian EMT annual program cohorts from 2018 to 2022 using National Registry of Emergency Medical Technicians Cognitive Examination data. We included cohorts with >5 candidates testing annually. Cohorts were grouped by fixed cohort size quartiles (Q) and National Association of State EMS Officials (NASEMSO) region. Outcomes were first- and cumulative third-attempt pass rates. Descriptive statistics summarized cohort characteristics and outcomes, and pairwise comparisons assessed group differences.

Results: Of 10,923 EMT educational program cohorts identified, 8567 (78.4%) were included. Median first- and cumulative-third attempt pass rates were 63.9% (interquartile rate [IQR]: 50.0, 77.7) and 77.8% (66.7, 88.3), respectively. Pass rates varied by cohort year, cohort size, and region. Median pass rates were highest in 2022. Q4 (≥46 candidates) had higher median first-attempt and third-attempt rates compared with Q1 (6-10) (first: 68.2%, 60.0%; third attempt: 81.6%, 71.4%). West NASEMSO region cohorts had higher median pass rates than all other regions.

Conclusion: From 2018 to 2022, EMT program success varied across cohort size, geographic region, and cohort year. Larger cohorts had higher median pass rates, and NASEMSO West cohorts had the highest median pass rates. These findings support continued EMT program evaluation and highlight the need for more education data to understand mechanisms for differences.
